An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.

paper_title: ATLAS-Bench: An Agentic Tool-Use Benchmark for Local Area Search
paper_abstract: Reliable local search is essential for LLM agents to support everyday decisions and longer plans by finding places that meet users' needs at given times and locations. Yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgments in place attributes and reviews. We introduce ATLAS-Bench, a benchmark of 1,200 queries across three regions, expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews, and existing user profiles from the platform. Each query distinguishes mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgments, with supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. We also introduce ATLASBox, a standardized evaluation environment with search tools and a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Given a query, timestamp, and location, an agent searches place attributes and reviews to recommend evidence-supported options or report that no place meets all mandatory requirements. We evaluate answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%). These results highlight the challenge of satisfying individual requirements while providing usable recommendations across queries.

paper_title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
paper_abstract: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.

paper_title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.

paper_title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases
paper_abstract: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.

paper_title: SymKL: A Unified Representation-Space Measure of Signal Degradation
paper_abstract: Quantifying degradation between a pristine signal and its degraded observation is fundamental to signal processing, yet existing full-reference measures are inherently modality-specific. We introduce SymKL, a unified full-reference degradation measure based on implicit neural representations (INRs). An INR is fitted once to the pristine reference and characterized by its diagonal Fisher information, which captures the local information geometry of the learned representation. Evaluating the Fisher information with the pristine reference and a degraded observation yields two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose symmetric KL divergence defines the degradation score. The proposed formulation requires only the reference and degraded observation, without knowledge of the corruption process or degradation severity, making it applicable across images, audio, and 3D data. We further derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of SIREN, enabling efficient computation. Experiments on image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks demonstrate that SymKL accurately tracks degradation severity, remains monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail, and provides a unified modality-agnostic measure of signal degradation. Code will be made publicly available after the review process.

paper_title: CASE: Concept-Aware Segmentation from Positive and Negative Visual Exemplars
paper_abstract: Few-shot semantic segmentation typically identifies target objects based on positive support examples of a single semantic class. In practice, however, positive cues alone are often underspecified: for instance, "red cars" may be confused with cars of all colors, "vehicles" may include cars that should be excluded, and "material-defined objects" may span multiple categories. Fulfilling precise requests requires positive exemplars to provide inclusion evidence and negative exemplars to act as intent-defining constraints for exclusion and disambiguation. We formulate this setting as Specified Visual Prompt Segmentation (SVPS), where the target concept is specified by both positive and negative visual prompts. In this work, visual exemplars refer to support-image regions specified by bounding-box prompts. To study SVPS, we introduce CASE (Concept-Aware Segmentation from Positive and Negative Visual Exemplars), a benchmark built on COCO and PACO. CASE encompasses six category- and attribute-level task families: exclusion, isolation, union, attribute exclusion, attribute isolation, and attribute union. We evaluate SAM 3 under this setting and find that, despite its powerful positive-only few-shot segmentation capability, frozen SAM 3 does not consistently treat negative visual prompts as exclusion evidence. To address this, we present Concept Prompt Adaptation (CPA), a conservative LoRA-based adaptation baseline that improves positive-negative prompt interpretation on CASE while remaining competitive under positive-only few-shot segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/WongKinYiu/FSS-CASE.

paper_title: LV SWARM Benchmarking Coordination Policies in a Lake Victoria Inspired Simulation
paper_abstract: Coordination policies can respond differently to depth structure, drifting targets and heterogeneous item mass in aquatic collection tasks. LV-SWARM represents these processes in a configured Lake Victoria-inspired simulation. This study analyses 700 archived trials covering twelve coordination mechanisms and two reference policies, with fifty seed labels per policy, twenty robots, six hundred initial items and a 2,000-second horizon. Collection fraction and simulated collected mass are compared using within-seed contrasts, bootstrap intervals and multiplicity-adjusted paired tests. Across the six environment-derived mechanisms, mean collection fraction was 4.77 percentage points lower than across the six general-purpose mechanisms (95% pointwise interval −5.40 to −4.11). The exploratory TSS–PDC–HPCA subset instead exceeded the general-purpose set by 7.50 percentage points (6.88 to 8.11). TSS had the highest median collection fraction, 0.6317, whereas HPCA had the highest median collected mass, 266.65 kg. Nine mechanisms exceeded the RANDOM reference in adjusted paired comparisons. Several comparisons with the myopic full-field SMOB reference did not detect a difference, but no equivalence margin was specified. A separate 100-trial MOUNS input ablation estimated a collection change of +1.14 percentage points (−1.48 to +3.70), leaving effects in either direction compatible with the results. These findings compare fixed implementations with unequal information access within one scenario. The environmental quantities are model assumptions, and the results establish neither field remediation performance nor ecological benefit. The archived records, analysis, figures and identified source snapshot are provided for computational reuse.

paper_title: 240 Children a Day: Tuberculosis Mortality at Ages 0–19 Years and the Widening Estimation Divide, 1990–2023
paper_abstract: Objectives: Tuberculosis (TB) in children is preventable and curable yet weakly diagnosed, notified, and monitored only to age 14 years. We analyzed the 0–19-year TB burden in the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023. Methods: We aggregated deaths and incident cases (95% uncertainty intervals [UIs]), 1990–2023, for four age bands across 204 countries, 21 regions and five Socio-demographic Index (SDI) quintiles; computed trends, pandemic-window changes with Monte Carlo–propagated uncertainty, and fixed-2021 SDI gradients, benchmarking against WHO estimates and End TB 2025 milestones. Results: In 2023, TB caused 87,764 deaths (95% UI 65,765–109,764) at ages 0–19 years—about 240 daily—and 1,665,272 incident cases; deaths fell 65.5% since 1990. Low- plus low-middle-SDI countries carried 90.3% of deaths across a 531-fold mortality gradient. GBD 0–14-year mortality was 39.9% of the like-for-like WHO estimate (66,146 vs 166,000); incidence agreed closely (80.8%). Deaths fell 23.9% over 2015–2023 against the 75% milestone. Adolescents aged 15–19 years improved slowest. Conclusions: Measurement systems disagree 2.5-fold on pediatric TB deaths, milestones are off track three-fold, and the burden concentrates where monitoring is weakest. Reconciling estimation, extending monitoring to ages 15–19 years, and concentrating resources on high-burden countries are prerequisites for ending TB in children.

paper_title: Beyond Predictive Accuracy: A Multidimensional Protocol for Business-Aware AI Recommendation Evaluation
paper_abstract: Predictive accuracy does not necessarily capture the economic or governance quality of AI-generated business recommendations. This exploratory study specifies a business-aware evaluation protocol covering incremental utility, downside risk, recommendation stability, and hard feasibility constraints, with a provisional composite index (BARQI). Previously executed repeated-split simulations in inventory, staffing, and manufacturing settings compare prediction-error selection, direct-utility selection, and risk-adjusted approaches. Across scenarios, downstream utility selection often improves on RMSE-based selection, while BARQI does not consistently outperform direct utility. Separately, eight constructed CMS-inspired pricing-transparency rule fixtures were classified as expected; this is a software unit-test result, not real regulatory compliance accuracy. A prospective validation protocol using the public UCI Online Retail II transaction dataset is specified, but raw data retrieval and empirical estimation have not been completed. The evidence supports transparent multidimensional reporting and falsifiable evaluation, not a claim that the proposed index is universally superior.

paper_title: Evaluation of the Association Between Periodontal Disease and Obesity in Adolescents from Puerto Rico: A Cross-Sectional Study
paper_abstract: Introduction: Adolescent obesity is a growing public health problem globally and is associated with multiple systemic and oral health consequences. Purpose: To estimate the prevalence of obesity and gingivitis in a sample of Puerto Rican adolescents, as well as to evaluate the possible association between both conditions. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 185 adolescents aged 13 to 20 years from five secondary schools. Each participant underwent a standardized dental examination to determine the presence of gingivitis by measuring periodontal probing depth and bleeding on probing, following NIDCR criteria. Body mass index was classified according to CDC guidelines. Statistical analyses included Pearson's chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, as well as multivariable generalized linear regression models. Results: The sample was predominantly female (61%), with a mean age of 15.7 years. Most participants had a healthy weight (48.7%), while 30.8% were classified as obese. After adjusting for age and sex, overweight and obesity were not significantly associated with bleeding on probing in ≥10% of sites (p = 0.25). However, overweight or obese adolescents were significantly more likely to have periodontal pockets ≥4 mm (OR = 2.1; 95% CI: 1.1–4.0, p = 0.03). Conclusion: No association was identified between obesity and gingivitis. Overweight and obesity were associated with early signs of periodontal disease.

paper_title: DRT-Assisted Evaluation of the Corrosion Inhibition of Vanillin on AA6082-T6 Aluminum Alloy
paper_abstract: The possibility to use vanillin for corrosion inhibition of AA6082-T6 aluminum alloy in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was investigated using AC/DC electrochemical techniques and quantitative metallography. DRT deconvolution demonstrated that uninhibited alloy dissolution is governed by mass-transfer-dominated mixed control, whereas vanillin adsorption preferentially blocks cathodic Al15(Fe,Mn)3Si2 and AlMnSi inclusions, shifting the corrosion process toward activation control. Pre-saturation adsorption obeyed the Langmuir isotherm with R2 = 0.9906 and free energy of adsorption of +27.63 kJ mol1, confirming mixed physisorption and chemisorption thermodynamically reinforced by electrolyte salting-out. At the optimal concentration of 1.0516 × 102 mol dm3, vanillin formed a protective 3D organic/inorganic interphase layer via bidentate chelation inside oxide pores and donor–acceptor coordination on Fe/Mn sites, reaching maximum inhibition efficiency of 82.94%. At higher concentration protection decreased to 71.82% due to supramolecular aggregation, a flat-to-vertical orientational transition, and ligand-promoted dissolution. Post-polarization surface analysis revealed that localized attack propagates radially along sub-grain boundaries, forming acidic occluded cells that sterically exclude bulky vanillin aggregates and prevent spontaneous repassivation.

paper_title: How Evaluation Protocol Shapes Reported Performance in CRISPR Guide-Efficiency Prediction
paper_abstract: Background. Reported area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in CRISPR guide-efficiency prediction depends on the binarisation threshold, the excluded fraction and the splitting unit. Both phenomena measured here have established names: spectrum bias, and type 1 and 2 circularity. We make no claim about how often these choices are reported. Three attempts to measure a reporting rate (Section 4.1) produced no defensible rate. Methods. For the protocol ladder we held one fixed model specification and one frozen out-of-fold prediction vector, assembled from five gene-grouped fold fits over 18,363 CRISPRi guides, and varied only the evaluation protocol. The comparisons across predictors, fold assignments and splits refit the models they name. Results. The reference span is 0.149 (0.137, 0.161): AUROC rises from 0.780 at the median split to 0.929 (top versus bottom 5%, 90% discarded). Under 40 alternative gene-to-fold assignments the mean 90%-cap AUROC is 0.926 and the mean span 0.147, and the deposited values exceed those of 37 of the 40, so the third decimal of the upper rungs is specific to the one deposited assignment. A Gaussian copula anchored to each predictor's median-split AUROC overshoots its protocol span by 37% to 63%, and every predictor's interval on that ratio excludes one. We tested only the Gaussian family. The margin between the linear baseline and the sequence-only boosted model falls from 0.014 at the median split to 0.003 at the 90% cap, not separable from zero from the 60% cap on, an observation we did not test against the copula's prediction. Per-gene conformal coverage is not distinguishable from calibration in aggregate, yet rises with guide count. Conclusions. Reported performance here is jointly determined by predictor and protocol. We release CRISPR-SCALE, an evaluation baseline under a fixed, fully stated protocol, reproducible within its pinned environment (Section 5).

paper_title: A Comparative Study on Performance Evaluation Systems and Career Development Support for Outstanding Faculty in Chinese and Kazakhstani Universities
paper_abstract: Amidst the ongoing restructuring of global higher education and the deepening of the “Belt and Road” initiative, retaining outstanding academic talent has become a crucial issue in Sino-Kazakh higher education cooperation. Drawing on organizational justice and perceived organizational support (POS) theories, this study examines the structural mechanisms linking performance evaluation, organizational support, and turnover intention. Based on a cross-sectional survey of 1,460 university faculty members (China n = 860; Kazakhstan n = 600), the findings indicate that faculty in both countries experience substantial evaluation pressure. While Chinese faculty report slightly higher perceived procedural justice, no significant cross-national differences emerged in distributive justice or emotional support. Results from hierarchical multiple regression and multi-group structural equation modeling (SEM) reveal that evaluation pressure positively predicts turnover intention, an association that is significantly stronger among Kazakhstani faculty navigating rapid institutional transitions and internationalization mandates. Furthermore, while organizational support does not directly buffer the negative effects of evaluation pressure, it is significantly associated with higher job satisfaction, thereby indirectly relating to lower turnover intention through a fully mediating pathway. This study expands the cross-cultural applicability of POS and organizational justice theories and offers targeted empirical insights for universities in transitional stages to optimize their performance accountability systems, reinforce career development support, and effectively mitigate academic talent attrition.

paper_title: Agentic AI Risk Evaluation Should Become a Continuous Assurance Discipline
paper_abstract: Language-model agents act through tools and credentials. A score from one tested configuration should not keep authorizing actions after the system, permissions, or threat model change. We argue that agentic AI is the first high-stakes domain in which assurance-invalidating change routinely outpaces evidence renewal. Continuous assurance is therefore not an improvement on benchmark evaluation, but a precondition for an authorization claim being true when it is relied upon. The machinery exists in nuclear, aviation, and medical-device regulation. Three requirements do not: a configuration baseline that makes change detectable, a change taxonomy calibrated to hazard relevance, and qualification criteria for evaluation environments. We propose the Agentic Assurance Stack (Stack), a versioned assurance profile linking each action path to a bounded claim, five evidence obligations, and a renewal rule.

paper_title: Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Language Models: A Survey of Costs, Trade-Offs, and Evaluation
paper_abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher behavior through feedback on student-generated trajectories. Its efficiency is often expressed in incompatible units: fewer examples, shorter rollouts, lower memory, higher throughput, or cheaper deployment. These gains need not coincide, and an inexpensive update need not minimize the cost of reaching a target capability. We survey efficient OPD through six connected tracks: data, rollout, teacher supervision, optimization, systems, and deployment amortization. A common accounting framework separates additive resource expenditure from elapsed time and peak memory, while preserving differences in state distributions, teacher access, and learning objectives. We accompany the synthesis with a versioned evidence ledger that records the workload, denominator, measurement boundary, and quality condition behind reported efficiency results. The resulting audit exposes several sources of non-comparability, including changed sequence caps, omitted preparation, stage-local memory statistics, and increased scoring cost hidden by faster generation. Building on existing general and formula-driven OPD surveys, our contribution is an operational organization of efficiency evidence and a reproducible cost-to-quality evaluation protocol. We conclude with testable research questions about budget allocation, state coverage, supervision value, and amortized deployment. The literature cutoff is October 25, 2026; no new model-training experiments are claimed.

paper_title: Pavement Crack Detection Based on an Improved YOLOv11 Network with CrackFormerV2 and Adaptive Threshold Focal Loss
paper_abstract: Pavement cracking is a common form of distress in asphalt pavements, and crack detection is essential for pavement maintenance. To improve detection accuracy in complex backgrounds, this study develops an enhanced YOLOv11-based detection algorithm. First, we construct CACrack2025, a pavement crack dataset that provides samples for model training and evaluation. Second, we design CrackFormerV2, a feature extraction module that combines cross-scale feature interaction with contextual information aggregation to improve the representation of slender, low-contrast cracks. To address the imbalance between crack targets and background regions, we incorporate Adaptive Threshold Focal Loss (ATFL), which reweights easy and hard classification samples according to their confidence. Experiments on CACrack2025 show that the proposed method achieves an mAP@50 of 86.0%, 4.6 percentage points higher than the baseline YOLOv11n model. Under the current dataset and evaluation protocol, the method maintains higher detection accuracy than the evaluated baselines. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed components for pavement crack detection.

paper_title: Risk-Calibrated Communication and Adaptive Safe Recovery in Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Under Compound Communication Failures
paper_abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) relies on communication to coordinate under partial observability. Real channels lose, delay, and corrupt messages, and a compromised agent can send misleading ones. In hierarchical MARL, these failures propagate into task-allocation errors and unsafe low-level actions. Prior work has studied message filtering, communication-constrained learning, and hierarchical recovery under message loss largely in isolation. This paper proposes RiCoR, a risk-calibrated communication and recovery framework for hierarchical MARL. RiCoR separates observable channel conditions from message credibility and represents uncertainty in its reliability estimates with an evidential Beta posterior. It gates each message by a lower confidence bound whose threshold rises with the downstream decision risk, measured by a conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) cost critic. A learned mode selector switches among normal coordination, selective reliance, active verification, and local fallback, with hysteresis and explicit switching and verification costs. A one-step safety shield filters low-level actions, and its guarantee is stated under explicit assumptions. The paper also specifies an evaluation protocol for a hierarchical wildfire-suppression benchmark with one coordinator and eight regional agents. The protocol covers isolated, compound, and held-out faults, four baselines, and calibration, recovery, ablation, scalability, and overhead analyses. The paper reports no empirical outcomes.

paper_title: Evaluation of Optical-Spectroscopy Based Identification of Breast Abnormality / Lumps in Indian Population Using Brexwel Device
paper_abstract: Background/Objectives: Female breast cancer has surpassed lung cancer as the most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and in India. In India, less than 5% of wom-en’s breast is screened per year due to limited medical and diagnostic facilities. 75% of female population with breast cancer is asymptomatic 1.e around 1.5 Lakh. Methods: The invention includes an integrated breast cancer screening device with pho-to-plethysmograpy based blood flow monitoring and thermal camera based hot-spot identification. The device is low-cost, non-invasive, portable, radiation-free with cloud-based validation by oncologist. The Near-IR based penetration within the wave-length 650 nm to 900 nm is sufficient to reach the breast tissue layers (beyond skin) to measure the change in oxygen consumption in normal and malignant breast tissues. Thermal imaging done by device help in measuring change in temperature in breast tissues based on thermophysical properties of blood flow in regions with malignancy. Results: Based on current sample size of 100 female subjects with breast problems, we have obtained accuracy above 80% and sensitivity above 90% using customized pro-tocol for data collection and analysis. Conclusions: This helps in identifying various breast problems that can turn into cancer, by custom-ized recommendation for follow-up by oncologists and doctors involved.

paper_title: Antidiabetic, Antioxidant, Anti-Inflammatory, and Organ-Protective Effects of Kura Mynis Polyherbal Formulation: In Vitro, Cellular, and In Vivo Evaluation in Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetic Rats
paper_abstract: Background: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disorder associated with persistent hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, inflammation, and progressive organ damage. The present study investigated the antidiabetic potential of Kura Mynis (KM), a novel polyherbal formulation containing multiple bioactive plant extracts with reported glucose-lowering, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties. Methods: The antidiabetic activity of KM was evaluated using in vitro α-amylase, α-glucosidase, xanthine oxidase, anti-inflammatory, and DPPH radical scavenging assays. Insulinotropic activity was assessed in MIN6 pancreatic β-cells, while cytotoxicity was determined using the MTT assay in HepG2 cells. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in streptozotocin-induced diabetic Wistar rats treated orally with KM (2055 and 4102 mg/kg) for 21 days. Blood glucose levels, body weight, lipid profile, liver function markers, and histopathological changes in pancreatic, hepatic, and renal tissues were assessed. Results: KM exhibited concentration-dependent inhibition of α-amylase (85%), α-glucosidase (58%), and xanthine oxidase (67%) at 100 µg/mL. Significant anti-inflammatory activity (44%) and potent antioxidant activity were observed, with 94.11% DPPH radical scavenging and an IC50 value of 86.93 µg/mL. KM enhanced insulin secretion in MIN6 cells by approximately 2.6-fold at 100 µg/mL without inducing cytotoxicity. In diabetic rats, KM significantly reduced fasting and postprandial blood glucose levels, improved body weight, and produced group-dependent modulation of serum transaminase and lipid parameters. Pancreatic, hepatic and renal histoarchitecture were substantially restored in a dose-dependent manner. Conclusion: KM exerts significant antidiabetic effects through multiple mechanisms, including enzyme inhibition, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, enhancement of insulin secretion, and histological preservation of pancreatic, hepatic and renal tissue. Effects on serum transaminases and lipids were modulatory and were not uniform across treatment groups. These findings support KM as a promising polyherbal candidate for diabetes management and its associated complications.

paper_title: Blockchain Security: A Reproducible Machine Learning Framework for Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection
paper_abstract: Smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain enable decentralized, trustless applications but remain highly susceptible to security vulnerabilities that have caused substantial financial losses. Traditional static and symbolic analysis tools often suffer from limited generalizability and high false-positive rates, motivating the exploration of machine learning alternatives. In this paper, we present a reproducible machine learning framework for smart contract vulnerability detection using a carefully designed synthetic dataset of 400 contracts. The dataset contains twelve static code-level features (including lines of code, external calls, delegatecalls, cyclomatic complexity, and state variable writes) and a binary vulnerability label with realistic class imbalance (22.5% vulnerable). We evaluate four classifiers Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting under a stratified train-test protocol. Experimental results show that tree-based ensembles achieve strong performance, with HistGradientBoosting reaching an F1-score of 0.971 and ROC-AUC of 1.000, while Logistic Regression provides a competitive and more interpretable baseline (F1-score 0.882, ROC-AUC 0.974). Feature importance analysis highlights external calls, delegatecalls, and cyclomatic complexity as the most discriminative indicators. We openly release the dataset, preprocessing pipeline, and evaluation scripts to support reproducibility. Although the synthetic nature of the data limits direct claims about real-world deployment, the framework offers a transparent, controllable testbed for benchmarking detection methods and studying the impact of class imbalance and feature design in smart contract security research.

paper_title: A Multi-Criteria Framework for the Ex Ante Evaluation of Development Projects in Highly Vulnerable Territories: Methodological Design from Canaan (Haiti)
paper_abstract: Development projects in highly vulnerable territories frequently underperform not because of poor technical design but because the organizational, territorial and contextual conditions required for implementation are not in place. In Canaan (Haiti), for example, many post-earthquake interventions were fragmented, duplicated one another and failed to deliver durable improvements, which is the practical problem addressed here. This article develops and operationalizes an ex ante multi-criteria framework, HEP-ZAV (an assessment tool for development projects in high-vulnerability zones), that assesses the suitability of a development project before implementation. Rather than treating weighting as the core task, the framework first transforms an integrated territorial diagnosis into a structured evaluation matrix of three levels, eleven factors and fifty-six sub-factors operationalized through indicators. The relative importance of the elements is established through a group Analytic Hierarchy Process with consistency and consensus diagnostics, and the model is implemented in a transparent decision-support tool that reports a three-component suitability profile instead of a single score. Because retrospective project data are unavailable, the behavior of the instrument is characterized through a Monte Carlo experiment of 100,000 projects and two sensitivity analyses, which show that, under the simulation assumptions, the three dimensions remain computationally separated and that the expert-derived weights increase score dispersion while the factor-importance ranking remains robust. The framework is a transferable ex ante screening instrument, not yet a validated predictor of project success.

paper_title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
paper_abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.

paper_title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry
paper_abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.

paper_title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
paper_abstract: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

paper_title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
paper_abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.
comments: Accepted to AACL 2026. This version corrects minor errors in the appendix

paper_title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
paper_abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

paper_title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
paper_abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

paper_title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
paper_abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.

paper_title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting
paper_abstract: Traffic forecasting requires modeling complex temporal dynamics and the spatial dependencies imposed by road topology. Supervised graph-based models achieve strong performance, but are often trained for a particular dataset and sensor graph, making deployment to new or evolving networks costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) offer a zero-shot alternative by learning in-context inference from synthetic task priors, which provide an explicit mechanism for encoding domain-specific assumptions. Existing forecasting PFNs, however, do not explicitly represent the graph-structured dependencies governing traffic dynamics. To combine graph-aware traffic modeling with zero-shot adaptation, we introduce the Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Network (GAS-PFN). GAS-PFN incorporates sampled road topology into its synthetic task prior through random-walk diffusion, teaching the model to learn graph-coupled dynamics during pretraining. Its co-designed inference architecture uses two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to separately model sensor-specific temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before integrating their representations for prediction. This design enables GAS-PFN to use target-network structure and context without parameter updates. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, GAS-PFN reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to TimePFN, its closest PFN-based predecessor. It also reduces MSE by 27.7% on average relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters. In this comparison, all models receive 90 minutes of contiguous recent history, and any additional context is drawn from each dataset's chronological training split. These results indicate that aligning PFN priors and inference architectures with graph structure improves in-context learning for zero-shot traffic forecasting.

paper_title: Timestral
paper_abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.

paper_title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
paper_abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

paper_title: ReferStream: Interactive Subject Injection for Streaming Video Generation
paper_abstract: Injecting new subjects naturally during streaming video generation requires integrating newly supplied visual references into the existing video while preserving established subjects and the scene. Encoding references independently of the current scene provides little guidance for this integration, while keeping their features in persistent memory can interfere with established context. We propose ReferStream, a framework that requires no additional training and combines reference construction using the current scene with transient cache injection. Joint Latent places reference latents in target regions of the latest scene latent, allowing reference features to be extracted in context. Cache Restoration uses these features to condition the injection chunk, then restores the overwritten global cache entries while retaining the newly generated history. This procedure incorporates new visual conditions without retraining the generator or revising emitted frames. We further introduce ReferStream Bench, a new benchmark with scheduled reference arrivals, evolving instructions, and explicit annotations of subject presence for InShot and MultiShot generation. Evaluation follows the event schedule and measures both the fidelity of new subjects and the preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality, text adherence, and count accuracy. Experiments on ReferStream Bench show higher scores for text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy than the compared baselines, including offline methods given all references in advance. Project page: https://xushuolin.github.io/ReferStream/.

paper_title: Pneuma: A Large-Scale Real-World Time Series Benchmark for Commercial Aircraft Predictive Maintenance
paper_abstract: Predictive maintenance is vital for commercial aviation, yet progress remains hindered by the lack of public, large-scale real-world datasets. As a result, most methods are developed and evaluated on proprietary data, limiting reproducibility. We introduce Pneuma, the first publicly available large-scale benchmark for predictive maintenance using onboard time series from in-service commercial aircraft. Built around bleed air systems, Pneuma contains over 920 million multivariate time steps across four aircraft types and 9 verified fault scenarios, directly aligned with real maintenance logs. The dataset exhibits key real-world challenges, including substantial class imbalance, subtle fault evolution patterns, and significant variance across aircraft configurations. We structure the benchmark around three tasks: multivariate forecasting, supervised fault classification, and unsupervised anomaly detection, with labels derived from actual maintenance records. Under unified settings, we evaluate over 25 models from four methodological families on 9 carefully curated subsets. The results reveal that even strong contemporary models struggle with subtle fault signatures. Further analyses show consistent gains from additional in-context examples and multivariate inference, while forecasting quality is strongly associated with anomaly detection performance. Together, these findings provide practical insights into effectively modeling complex real-world aviation time series. We hope Pneuma will serve as a rigorous and reproducible foundation for advancing data-driven predictive maintenance toward real-world deployment in commercial aviation.

paper_title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
paper_abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.

paper_title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
paper_abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

paper_title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping
paper_abstract: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training pairs.
comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. 15 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, including references and appendices

paper_title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
paper_abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

paper_title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
paper_abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 10 pages main text, 33 pages total. Code: https://github.com/hannesill/m4/tree/m4bench-neurips2026-camera-ready/benchmark . Evidence: https://huggingface.co/datasets/hannesill/m4bench-evidence

paper_title: Graph Representation Learning via Adaptive Expectile Aggregation
paper_abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely critically on neighborhood aggregation, yet conventional mean aggregation may fail to capture class-relevant distributional information, particularly in heterophilic graphs. We propose ExpectileGCN, an adaptive graph aggregation framework that introduces a learnable expectile level to capture neighborhood information beyond the mean. The proposed operator continuously adjusts aggregation between minimum- and maximum-type behaviors, with mean aggregation as a special case. A differentiable approximation based on sigmoid smoothing and fixed-point iterations enables end-to-end optimization. Theoretically, we establish stability properties and transductive generalization guarantees for ExpectileGCN. We further investigate its classification risk under heterophilic neighborhood models. For informative neighborhoods, we show that expectile aggregation can exploit class-dependent scale differences to achieve a classification advantage over mean aggregation. Under a local asymptotic regime with diminishing per-neighbor label informativeness, we establish that this advantage can persist in terms of limiting classification risk. Experiments on homophilic and heterophilic benchmark graphs demonstrate strong predictive performance and improved robustness under feature corruption and structural perturbations.

paper_title: Representing the Unseen: Rethinking Visual Imagination for Spatial Reasoning
paper_abstract: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.

paper_title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features
paper_abstract: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.

paper_title: When Visual Evidence Is Insufficient: How Instructions, Post-Training, and Internal Activations Shape Refusal in Multimodal Language Models
paper_abstract: For reliable deployment, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) should recognize when an image provides insufficient evidence to answer a question and withhold unsupported answers. Yet refusal alone is not necessarily evidence of such recognition: models may refuse because of unrelated safety constraints or without identifying the missing evidence. We study how refusal on visually unanswerable questions is shaped by three sources of control: inference-time instructions, post-training, and internal activation interventions. Across three MLLMs on the MoHoBench benchmark, we systematically manipulate the meaning and placement of refusal instructions, compare supervised and preference-based post-training, and intervene on a refusal-related activation direction derived from naturally answered and refused examples. We find that refusal is highly sensitive to both the meaning and placement of instructions, with model-specific changes at the sample level that are obscured by aggregate refusal rates. Evidence-aware and general refusal instructions have stronger effects than an intentionally mismatched safety instruction. Post-training produces larger increases in refusal, but can also induce responses that combine refusal language with attempted answers. In contrast, activation intervention produces smaller yet transferable changes across prompt conditions, without evidence of indiscriminate refusal on tested visually answerable samples. These findings show that refusal is jointly shaped by external instructions, post-training, and internal representations, highlighting the need to disentangle evidence recognition from a model's learned propensity to refuse.

paper_title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
paper_abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations.   A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral.   The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.

paper_title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

paper_title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
paper_abstract: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. That limits the validation of generative models to standard goodness-of-fit tests, in which the generative model is treated as exact (point-null hypothesis). But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We propose SIGMA, an end-to-end framework combining density estimation with principled uncertainty quantification. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

paper_title: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution
paper_abstract: Language model performance depends strongly on the mixture of domains in the pretraining data corpus. Popular data mixing methods select these domain weights by training many small proxy models on random mixes and then fitting a regression model to predict performance from the mix. We recognize this practice as a domain attribution problem, where the regression measures each domain's contribution to the target metric. Through this lens, the standard Dirichlet sampling of proxy data mixes is a poor regression design that requires tuning and cannot support a linear fit for hundreds of domains. Building on classical optimal experimental design, we introduce LinMix, which samples mixes at the vertices of the capped simplex so that each domain is at its cap or absent. This hyperparameter-free vertex sampling decorrelates domain effects, enabling an interpretable linear model whose coefficients are the domain attributions. The optimal mix given by LinMix provably keeps only domains with positive attribution values and requires no search over candidate mixes. We further establish the optimality of vertex sampling, and prove that Dirichlet sampling inflates the attribution error when its mixes concentrate around the prior data mix. Pretraining experiments with 1B-parameter OLMo2 and 4B Qwen3.5 language models show that LinMix outperforms Dirichlet-based data mixing across reasoning, code, and math benchmarks, with relative gains of 46% on MBPP and 14% on GSM8K. At 288 fine-grained domains, only vertex sampling supports a linear fit, and LinMix improves benchmark accuracy by 11% on average over the best nonlinear baseline.
comments: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale

paper_title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
paper_abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

paper_title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
paper_abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited.
